analysis: All Light, anchored and Rajagopalan-Schulman (40 rounds) verdicts are correct on 90 instances (n = 32..512). Certification of associative inputs - the exhaustive check costs 23-383 (cyclic) and 38-614 (anchored) times more table probes than Light's test with a greedy generating set (generating-set cost included), but only 1.7 times more on left-zero bands (x*y = x, every element is a generator). Refutation - an exhaustive check stopping at the first violating triple needs 4 probes on random magmas and 0.1-1.1 times Light's probes on one-entry corruptions. Random-triple sampling with n^2/16 samples misses 27 of the 30 inputs that differ from an associative table in one entry (about 4n bad triples out of n^3). At n = 512 (shared machine, indicative) - exhaustive 1.3-1.7 s for associative inputs, Light 2-3 ms + 3 ms for the generating set, anchored test 3 ms, RS(40) 0.15 s. (Re-run after the Skeptic's review with corrected probe accounting; the first version charged the exhaustive check a whole 64-row slab on non-associative inputs.)
assumptions: n in {32, 64, 128, 256, 512}; 3 instances per randomised family
probes = table look-ups (machine-independent cost); wall times are medians of 3 runs on a shared, loaded machine and are indicative only
families: cyclic group Z_n, anchored x+y+1, left-zero band x*y = x (needs all n generators), the first two with one corrupted entry, random magmas
counterexamples: left-zero band x*y = x: Light's test needs n generators and is only 1.7x cheaper than the exhaustive check (H-C17-1 refuted)
falsification: H-C17-1: a family where Light's test costs more than 10/n of the exhaustive probes. H-C17-3: a wrong verdict of the randomised test.

hypothesis: H-C17-1 (bold): Light's test with a greedy generating set beats the exhaustive test by a factor >= n/10 in table probes on every input family. H-C17-3: the Rajagopalan-Schulman test with 40 rounds never errs on the benchmark (one-sided error <= (7/8)^40 per non-associative input).
methodology: Run every algorithm on every instance; record verdict, probes, time; compare with the exhaustive verdict; for random triples use a budget of n^2/16 samples to expose its failure mode on near-associative inputs. The exhaustive check is charged the probes of a sequential check that stops at the first violating triple (revised after the Skeptic's review - the first version charged a whole 64-row slab, so its ratios on non-associative inputs measured the slab size). Probe ratios are reported separately for associative inputs (certification, where every test must do its full work) and non-associative inputs (refutation).
question: How much cheaper than the exhaustive n^3 check are generator-based, anchored and randomised associativity tests, on which inputs, and with which error rates?
